clips.text:
When to use Assalamualaikum.
You are standing at the door of a Malaysian friend's house, or sliding into the back seat of a Grab, or walking into a mamak at 11pm. You have one greeting to choose and about two seconds to choose it. Get it wrong and nothing explodes — but at someone's door it lands as a small slight, and you will feel it.
Your phrasebook (section 2, Greetings and basics) gives you the two options side by side: Read the Notes column carefully, because it is doing more work than it looks. Assalamualaikum is an Arabic loan that means "peace be upon you". It is a religious greeting — a Muslim greets another Muslim with it.
In Malaysia it has also become a general courtesy greeting, used well outside Muslim company: a non-Muslim shopkeeper will often open with it, and a non-Muslim is not expected to be offended by hearing it. What follows from that is the part people get wrong.
You say it when you are the one greeting, and you are reasonably confident the person you are greeting is Muslim. You do not say it back to someone who did not say it to you, and you do not use it as a neutral default for a stranger whose religion you cannot guess. That is what Helo is for.
If someone greets you with Assalamualaikum, the reply is fixed: Waalaikumussalam — "and peace be upon you too". It is not optional and it is not a different greeting; it is the second half of the same exchange. You can say it whether or not you are Muslim. It is a courtesy, not a conversion.
Pronunciation, from section 1 of the same phrasebook: s is a normal s, a is the "a" in father (softening to "uh" at the end of a word in everyday Peninsular speech), and the final m is a full hummed m — as-sa-la-mu-a-lai-kum, six syllables, stress light and even. Waalaikumussalam is longer: wa-a-lai-ku-mus-sa-lam.
Do not swallow the double s in the middle; that doubled consonant is the seam between kum and salam. Two body conventions come with the greeting, and you will meet both in your first week. The right hand. When you shake hands, pass food, hand over money or take a receipt, use your right hand, or both hands.
The left hand is reserved for hygiene. A Grab driver passing your change, a mamak waiter setting down your teh tarik, a lecturer accepting your assignment — right hand. If you are carrying something in your right hand, use both hands rather than the left alone. Shoes.
Shoes come off before you enter a Malaysian home, and before you step into a mosque or a surau. Look for the shoe rack at the door; if there is one, that is the instruction. Socks stay on.
If you are unsure whether a place is a shoes-off place, look at what your host is wearing on their feet — that answers it faster than asking. One more thing worth knowing before you open your mouth: a handshake with someone of the opposite sex may not be offered.
A Muslim woman may greet a man with a small nod and a hand over the heart instead of an outstretched hand. That is a complete greeting, not a rejection. Mirror it: nod, hand on heart, smile, and say your greeting.
The greeting decision runs in two directions. When you speak first, you choose. When they speak first, the reply is already decided for you.
Think of Assalamualaikum the way you think of "Merry Christmas" in a mixed office in December. Most people will smile and say it back; a few will say "Happy holidays"; nobody is insulted that you offered it. It is a warm, specific greeting that has leaked out of its original community into general polite use.
Now think about the difference between offering it and assuming it. You say "Merry Christmas" to a colleague whose Christmas you know about. You do not open every December meeting with it to a room of strangers, because a handful of them will spend the next ten minutes deciding whether you were being careless.
Helo is your "good morning, everyone". The analogy breaks the moment you treat the reply as optional. "Merry Christmas" has no fixed second half — you can answer it with a smile, a nod, or "you too". Assalamualaikum does.
It is a call-and-response pair, and leaving the response hanging is the one thing that reads as a snub rather than as a neutral choice. The analogy also fails on the body: there is no hand-over-the-heart equivalent in the office, and no shoes-off rule at the conference room door.
Assalamualaikum is the Malaysian version of "hello", so I should use it everywhere to show I have made an effort with the local language. It is a Muslim greeting that has spread into general courtesy use, not a religion-neutral hello. The people you hear using it are mostly Muslim and mostly greeting other Muslims.
When you are the one speaking first and you do not know the person's religion, Helo is the correct choice — it is listed in the same phrasebook table for exactly this reason.
The difference shows up at a door: greeting a non-Muslim host with Assalamualaikum is not offensive, but it is noticeably off, in the way that being greeted in a language you do not belong to is off.
And if someone greets you with it, the reply is fixed at Waalaikumussalam regardless of your own religion — that half is never optional.
It is your fourth day in Malaysia. You have been invited to your tutor's house for Raya open house, along with six other students. You are at the gate. Your tutor, Puan Farah, opens the door and says "Assalamualaikum, masuk, masuk."
Behind her you can see a shoe rack with about a dozen pairs of shoes on it, and a tiled floor.
Assalamualaikum is a Muslim greeting that has spread into general courtesy use in Malaysia; it is not a religion-neutral hello. When you speak first and do not know the other person's religion, Helo is the correct choice — it sits in the same phrasebook table for exactly that reason.
If someone greets you with Assalamualaikum, the reply is Waalaikumussalam, and you say it whether or not you are Muslim. Assalamualaikum is six syllables with a full hummed final m; Waalaikumussalam keeps the doubled s in the middle, at the seam between kum and salam.
Shake hands, pass food and hand over money with the right hand or both hands; the left hand is reserved for hygiene. Shoes come off before entering a Malaysian home, a mosque or a surau — the shoe rack at the door is the instruction.
A small nod with a hand over the heart instead of an outstretched hand is a complete greeting, not a rejection; mirror it rather than reaching.
Think of the last time someone greeted you in a way you did not expect — a language you do not speak, a formality you were not prepared for, a hand you did not take. What did you actually do in the two seconds before you decided?
Now decide, in advance, what your two seconds will look like the next time a Malaysian greets you first: which word comes out, and what your hands are doing while it does.
Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus.

How Malay sounds and how it is spelled.
Malay uses the same 26 letters you already read. The trap is that it uses them differently. English e has several sounds; Malay e has two. English c is sometimes k, sometimes s; Malay c is always the ch in church.
Read terima kasih with English vowel rules and you get "teh-RYE-mah KAY-see" — nobody in a mamak will turn around. Read it with the table below and you get "tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh", which works. Two rules carry most of the load.
Vowels are short and pure. a is the a in father, i is ee in see, u is oo in food, o is o in low with no w sliding off the end. No diphthongs — do not glide.
Consonants are single-valued. c is always ch. g is always hard, as in go — never the soft g of giant. j is the j in jug. ng is the ng in singer, with no hard g after it; ngg is the ng in finger, with one. ny is the ny in canyon. sy is sh. kh is the Scottish ch in loch. Two endings need practice.
A word-final -a softens to a short uh in everyday Peninsular speech: saya is "sa-yuh", not "sa-yah". And a word-final -k is not a k at all — it is a stop in the throat, the sound you make in the middle of "uh-oh". tidak comes out "tida'" with the mouth closing and nothing released. Stress is light and even.
Most speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable, but leaning wrong costs you far less than mispronouncing a c or a final a.
Your phrasebook lists terima kasih (thank you). Here is the whole word taken apart with the table, letter group by letter group. Put together: tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh. Stress sits lightly on the second-last syllable of each word — tuh-REE-mah, KAH-seeh.
Now the same method on a word you will meet at the counter. ais (iced) is not English "ace": a is a in father, i is ee, so it is "ah-ees", two syllables, not one. And kopi is "ko-pee", not "KOH-pye".
Run the method on any new word: split it, apply the table to each chunk, then check the two endings — a final -a softens, a final -k stops.
Malay is written in the Latin alphabet, so I can just read it the way I read English. Malay shares the alphabet but not the letter values. c is always ch, never k or s. g is always hard. Word-final a softens to uh and word-final k becomes a throat stop.
Read terima kasih with English rules and you produce "teh-RYE-mah KAY-see"; read it off the table and you produce "tuh-ree-mah kah-seeh". The difference predicts whether a mamak counter understands you on the first try or the third.
Pick three Malay words you have already seen this week — on a sign, a menu, a Grab receipt. Sound each one out with the table before you check it against anything. Which letter was the one you got wrong, and which row of the table would have caught it?

Greeting people, introducing yourself, what to call them.
You are standing at the counter of a mamak at 8am. The man behind it is roughly your father's age. You open your mouth and out comes awak — the word you drilled last night for "you".
His face does not change, but the transaction does: he answers you in English for the rest of the order, and you have just told him, in his own language, that the two of you are peers. Malay has two systems running side by side, and the one you pick is a social decision, not a grammar decision.
The neutral set is what a stranger uses. Saya for I, awak for you when you are clearly the same age or younger, anda for you on signs, forms and in formal writing. For a stranger you cannot place, use a title instead of "you": Encik (any adult man), Puan (a married or older woman), Cik (a young woman).
These are the words in your phrasebook table, and they are safe because they carry no claim about the relationship. The kinship set is what Malaysians actually reach for.
Pak cik (uncle) for a man old enough to be your father, mak cik (auntie) for a woman the same, abang (older brother) for a man a few years older, kakak (older sister) for a woman a few years older. These are not literal family. A mamak uncle is a pak cik on first meeting. The Grab driver who is 30 is an abang.
The woman at the campus counter is a kakak. The rule that keeps you out of trouble: when you can see the person, kinship beats pronoun. Awak is for someone you have already established as a peer — a classmate, someone your age who has introduced themselves. Used on a pak cik, it reads as a demotion.
Used on a kakak at the faculty office, it reads as a student who has not learned where they are. The phrasebook table in section 2 of your phrasebook gives you Siapa nama awak? and Nama saya Oybek. — note that the model sentence uses awak, because it is written for peer-to-peer introductions.
When you introduce yourself to a pak cik, you swap the pronoun for the kinship word and the rest of the sentence does not move: Siapa nama pak cik? / Nama saya Oybek. Greetings layer on top of this.
Selamat pagi until about noon, selamat tengah hari around midday, selamat petang from mid-afternoon until dusk, selamat malam after dark. Helo works at any hour and carries no religious weight. Assalamualaikum is the Muslim greeting you will hear often; the reply is Waalaikumussalam.
If you are unsure, Helo is never wrong. Two more words do more work than their length suggests. Terima kasih is thank you; terima kasih banyak is thank you very much, and it is what you say to a pak cik who has just walked your order to the table.
Maaf covers both sorry and excuse me; minta maaf is the fuller apology you use when you have actually done something — knocked a drink over, arrived late to a tutorial.
Four ways to say "you" in Malay. They are not interchangeable, and the deciding factor is not politeness in the abstract — it is who is standing in front of you and how you need to be read. the tutorial group chat, the friend you met at orientation, anyone who has already used your first name.
any written message where you do not know the reader. Face to face, prefer Encik, Puan or Cik. every food stall, every shop counter, every older neighbour for your entire first month. the Grab driver, the senior at the faculty office, the barista who looks 25.
The same transaction, run three times. The only thing that changes is the word for "you". Setup. It is 8:15am. The stall is run by a man in his fifties. You want roti canai and teh tarik. You have learned Siapa nama awak? and Nama saya Oybek. from section 2 of your phrasebook.
Attempt 1 — the phrasebook sentence, unchanged. You: Selamat pagi. Siapa nama awak? Pak cik: Selamat pagi. [in English] What would you like? He answered the greeting in Malay and the question in English. Awak told him you were addressing him as a peer, and he corrected the register by switching languages.
Nothing rude happened, but you lost the exchange. Attempt 2 — kinship swapped in. You: Selamat pagi, pak cik. Siapa nama pak cik? Pak cik: Selamat pagi. [name]. Nak apa? Nak apa? is "what do you want?" — the standard next move. You have been read as a polite student, and he is now speaking Malay to you.
Attempt 3 — the full order. You: Selamat pagi, pak cik. Saya nak roti canai satu, teh tarik satu. Pak cik: Boleh. (food arrives) You: Terima kasih banyak, pak cik. Pak cik: Sama-sama. What changed between 1 and 3. Not vocabulary — you used selamat pagi and terima kasih in all three.
The single substitution of awak to pak cik is what moved the conversation from English back into Malay, and terima kasih banyak rather than plain terima kasih is what closes it. Note also that saya never changes: it is safe in every one of the three attempts.
The pronoun that carries risk is the one for the other person, not the one for you.
Awak is just the polite word for "you", so I should use it with everyone until I know them well enough for something more casual. Awak is the peer word, not the polite word. It asserts that you and the person you are addressing are on the same level, and it is the correct default only for someone your own age.
Addressing a pak cik — a man old enough to be your father — as awak is not a grammar error, it is a social one: you have claimed equality with him. The phrasebook's model sentence is written for peer-to-peer introductions, which is why it uses awak; the moment the person in front of you is a generation older, the sentence stays and the pronoun swaps to pak cik.
The difference predicts the response: use awak on a mamak uncle and he answers in English; use pak cik and he keeps speaking Malay.
It is your third day. You are at the mamak near campus at 8am. The stall is run by a man in his fifties. You want roti canai and teh tarik. You have learned: selamat pagi, saya, awak, pak cik, terima kasih, terima kasih banyak, maaf, minta maaf.
Helo, saya dah sampai. Awak di mana?
Baik, semua faham? Tugasan pertama perlu dihantar minggu depan.

What BMK 2 at Taylor's actually is.
My phrasebook is my BMK 2 syllabus — if I learn the phrases, I've covered the module. BMK 2 is an assessed module with its own code, credit value and category; the phrasebook is unassessed practice that supports it.
The difference predicts which one shows up on your transcript: the phrasebook never does, and skipping the module's own requirements costs you credits regardless of how well you order at a mamak.
BMK 2 is not a phrasebook. It is a module on your degree record, and it has a code, a credit value and a category, the same way your programme's other modules do. Module code: MPU31002. That is the code to look for when you register and on your timetable. Learn it as a string, not as a description. 2 credits.
It carries two credits toward your degree. Two credits sounds small, which is exactly why it is easy to treat as optional. It is not optional: MPU modules are compulsory, and Taylor's says students must take all the MPU modules listed under each category. It sits in the MPU group.
MPU (Mata Pelajaran Pengajian Umum) modules are the compulsory general-studies modules of Malaysian higher education, taken alongside your programme. They are not a Taylor's invention and not a language-school add-on: they are a national requirement that Taylor's delivers.
Taylor's groups MPU modules into categories U1 to U4. For international degree students, BMK 2 sits in U1, next to Kursus Integriti dan Antirasuah and Citra Malaysia. Malaysian students take different U1 modules instead of BMK 2, so your BMK class is made up of international students like you.
The practical consequence: BMK 2 is assessed. Your phrasebook is not. Use the phrasebook to survive the mamak, the Grab and the campus — and use it to arrive at BMK 2 already able to say something. Then let the module itself tell you what it assesses.
Module name, code, credits and category are as listed on Taylor's MPU page on 10 October 2026; check that page for the current list.
Bahasa Melayu Komunikasi 2 is a module on your degree record, not a phrasebook or a club. Its module code is MPU31002. It carries 2 credits, so it counts toward the degree even though the number is small. It is an MPU module: MPU modules are the compulsory general-studies modules of Malaysian higher education.
For international degree students at Taylor's it sits in category U1; Malaysian students take different U1 modules instead. The module is assessed; your phrasebook is unassessed practice that supports it. Learning phrases helps you in class, but it does not stand in for completing the module.
Where on your own registration or timetable does MPU31002 appear, and what does the entry next to it say? Find it before your next BMK 2 class.

Capstone: a full day in Malay.
You have the phrases. What you do not have is a day where you used them. The failure mode this capstone prevents is specific. You order at a mamak in English, it works, and you conclude that Malay is optional. Six months later you still cannot say teh tarik kurang manis, satu without rehearsing it in your head first.
The first attempt will feel clumsy. Clumsy is the point. Today you run three scenes from your phrasebook in one short day: Mamak breakfast — order a drink and food, ask for the bill. Grab ride to campus — greet the driver, confirm the destination, thank them.
One conversation on campus — introduce yourself, ask one real question. Before you leave, write your lines down. Not because you will read them, but because writing them commits you to a specific sentence instead of a vague intention.
Use only the phrases from your phrasebook — teh tarik kurang manis, satu, roti canai satu, kuah campur, bang, kira, terima kasih, bang — spelled as your phrasebook spells them. After each scene, log one line: which Malay phrase you actually said, and which one you abandoned for English.
The abandoned ones are your real syllabus for next week. Your phrasebook notes that final k is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — tidak sounds like "tida'". Say your lines out loud once before you go. Stress is light and fairly even, so do not hunt for an English-style emphasis.
Fifteen minutes of preparation, then you go. Do this the evening before or the morning of — not in the queue. Pick your three scenes and write the lines. On paper or in your notes app, write three headings: Mamak, Grab, Campus. Under each, write the exact Malay lines you intend to say, copied from your phrasebook.
Mamak, from section 5: Teh tarik kurang manis, satu. Then Roti canai satu, kuah campur. Then, at the end, Bang, kira. Grab, from section 6: Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus. as you get in, then Terima kasih, bang on arrival. Campus, from section 7: Saya pelajar antarabangsa.
Then one question — Di mana perpustakaan? or Boleh saya duduk di sini? Say every line out loud twice. Read each line aloud. Twice. Your phrasebook notes that final k is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — so tidak comes out like "tida'".
Stress is light and fairly even; many speakers lean slightly on the second-last syllable. Say terima kasih, bang until the bang does not sound like the English word "bang". Order at the mamak. The waiter will ask Nak minum apa? — what would you like to drink. Answer with your written line: Teh tarik kurang manis, satu.
They will then ask Makan? — anything to eat. Answer: Roti canai satu, kuah campur. When you are done, get attention and say Bang, kira. They will name the price, e.g. Empat ringgit lima puluh sen — RM 4.50. Pay, then Terima kasih, bang! Take the Grab and use your Malay lines.
Get in and say Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus. When you are close, Tolong berhenti di sini. On arrival, Terima kasih, bang. Even one of these lines, said out loud to a real person, counts. One campus conversation. Find one person — classmate, staff, anyone — and say Saya pelajar antarabangsa.
Then ask your one question: Di mana perpustakaan? or Boleh saya duduk di sini? If they answer in English, that is fine. You still opened in Malay. Log what you abandoned. Within an hour of finishing, write three short entries: scene, phrase you said, phrase you dropped for English.
Be honest — the dropped ones are the ones you will drill next week.
You are at a mamak for breakfast. The waiter comes to your table. Order a drink and food, then ask for the bill.
Run the day described in this lesson: mamak breakfast, Grab ride to campus, one campus conversation. Then write it up. Constraints. Every Malay line you report must appear in your phrasebook, spelled as your phrasebook spells it. Do not invent sentences. The day must include all three scenes.
A day with only the mamak does not count. Report what actually happened, including the lines you abandoned. A log with no abandoned lines is almost certainly not honest. What "done" looks like A short written log with three sections — one per scene.
Each section names the Malay lines you said, the lines you dropped for English, and one sentence on what you would say differently next time. Finish with a three-line list of the phrases you are drilling next week.
This fits in one 15-minute sitting after the day itself: the day takes the time, the write-up takes the sitting.

Grab, directions and getting to campus.
The Grab arrives. You get in. Neither of you says anything useful for eleven minutes, and you spend the whole ride hoping the pin was right. That silence is the thing this lesson removes. It is not a vocabulary problem — you already know enough words.
It is a sequencing problem: the ride has four moments where something must be said, and if you say them in the wrong order or skip one, the driver fills the gap with his own guess. The four moments, in order: When he calls or texts — tell him where you are standing, in a way he can act on.
Before he moves — confirm the destination out loud, even though the app already shows it. This is your best chance to catch a wrong pin while the car is still stationary. While moving — give directions only if he asks or if he is clearly about to miss the turn.
On arrival — stop him at the right gate, not at the security post 400 metres earlier. Your source phrasebook has all of these in section 6. What it does not give you is the order, and the order is what stops the silent ride. Two things about how the words sound, from section 1 of the same phrasebook.
Final k is a short stop in the throat, not a full "k" — so tidak comes out closer to "tida'". And stress is light and fairly even, leaning slightly on the second-last syllable. That matters here because belok and terus are the two words a driver has to catch over engine noise, and both are short.
One structural note before you start. On campus, the same three direction words do all the work: kiri, kanan, terus. You will use them on foot, in a car, and pointing at a map on someone's phone. Learn them once, here.
The full ride, from booking to getting out, in the order it happens: first the driver has to find you, then you confirm where you are going, then you steer and stop. When he calls, describe where you are standing. Drivers often call rather than text. Answer, and say where you are: Saya tunggu di pintu utama.
Then add one thing he can see from the road: Saya pakai baju biru. If you are not there yet: Saya lambat sikit, lima minit. Swap biru for whatever colour you are actually wearing. The colour is the whole point — it is the only part of this that he can use from a moving car.
Ask whether he has arrived, once, if the car is not where you are. If the app says the car is here and you cannot see it, send: Abang dah sampai? Abang is the friendly address for a man a bit older than you — the same bang you use for the mamak waiter. It is the right word for a Grab driver too. Send it once.
If he does not reply within a minute, call. Do not send it three times; a driver who is circling a one-way system cannot read while driving, and repeated messages make him stop reading altogether. Get in and say the destination out loud. As you open the door or just after you sit down, say:
Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus. This is the phrase from section 6 of your phrasebook. You are not asking a question — you are stating the destination so he can confirm it. If he repeats it back or nods, you are aligned.
If he says something you do not catch, point at his phone screen and say ini while tapping the pin. Say it before the car moves. A wrong pin corrected at the kerb costs ten seconds; corrected 3 km down the road it costs a fare and an argument. Give directions only when he asks or is about to miss a turn.
Three words, from section 6: And if he overshoots: Pusing balik. Say the word, then point. The gesture and the word together survive engine noise; either one alone often does not.
Your phrasebook notes that Wikivoyage also lists Pusing kiri and Pusing kanan for left and right — if a driver uses those, they mean the same thing, and belok is the safer word to produce yourself. If he asks how long: Berapa lama? is the question, and Jalan sesak or Jem is what he will say back if the answer is bad.
Stop him at the right gate. When you can see where you want to get out: Tolong berhenti di sini. Say it early enough that he can pull over legally. On a campus road that means roughly 50 metres before the point you actually want, because he needs to find a gap. If you are not sure whether you are close enough yet, ask:
Dekat atau jauh? using dekat and jauh from the same table. On foot, use the same three words. The direction words do not change when you get out of the car. If you are lost on campus and stop someone: Di mana perpustakaan? Then listen for kiri, kanan or terus in the answer.
Those three are the whole of what you need to catch. If the answer comes too fast, say the place again and point — most people will point as they repeat it, and the point is the answer. Di mana perpustakaan? is from section 7 of your phrasebook; the rest of the campus words come in the campus lesson.
You booked a Grab to Taylor's Lakeside Campus. The app says the car has arrived. You are at the main entrance in a blue shirt. The driver is somewhere nearby and cannot see you.
The app already shows the driver my destination, so saying it out loud is redundant. The pin is where you dropped it, which is not always where you are going. Campuses have several gates, and a pin dropped on the wrong side of a dual carriageway still routes somewhere.
Saying Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's, Lakeside Campus before the car moves costs four seconds and surfaces the mismatch while the car is stationary. The difference it predicts: if you skip it, the first time you learn the pin was wrong is when the car stops somewhere you do not recognise, and by then you are negotiating a fare in a language you have had for two weeks.
Take one actual Grab trip you will make in the next few days — campus to a mamak, campus to KL Sentral, or a ride back to your accommodation. Before you book it, write the four things you will say, in Malay, in the order you will say them: the location line, the destination line, one direction line for a turn you expect on that route, and the stop line.
Constraints: Every Malay phrase must come from section 6 of your phrasebook, spelled exactly as it appears there (swapping in your own shirt colour is fine). Do not compose new Malay sentences.
The location line must contain something specific to you: the gate you will actually stand at, or the colour shirt you will actually wear. The direction line must name a real turn on the route, not a generic one. Look at the map before you write it. Then take the ride and say all four.
Done means you have said all four out loud to a real driver, and you can state which one he responded to fastest.

On campus and in your BMK class.
On the Grab ride in you learned to say Saya nak pergi ke Taylor's. That gets you to the gate. It does not get you through a lecture. The gap is not vocabulary.
It is that a BMK class moves at the speed of the room, and if you never say anything, the tutor will keep going and you will sit through the whole class understanding nothing. Three phrases stop that: Saya tak faham. — I don't understand. Boleh ulang? — Can you repeat that?
Boleh cakap perlahan sikit? — Can you speak a bit slower? Your phrasebook lists all three in its basics table, and they are the ones that keep a class from running past you. A tutor who hears Saya tak faham will rephrase. A tutor who hears nothing assumes you followed. Two habits make these work.
First, Minta maaf before the request — it is more polite than plain maaf, and you are interrupting. Second, say the phrase even when you half-understood. Half-understanding is the state you are trying to escape, and it looks identical to full understanding from the front of the room.
For the lecturer, one sentence carries the whole introduction: Saya pelajar antarabangsa. Add where you are from and what you study and you are done — Saya dari Uzbekistan. Saya belajar sains komputer. For buildings, the pattern is Di mana plus the place.
Di mana perpustakaan? works for the library, the admin office, the toilet. For class timing, Bila kelas mula? And when a word goes past you, do not nod. Ask Apa maksud "tugasan"? — tugasan is assignment, and it will appear on every brief you get this semester.
It is the first week of your BMK class. The tutor has just explained the assessment structure at speed, in Malay, and you caught about a third of it. Class is still running. You need to stop it from running past you — without derailing the whole room.
How to actually do this in the room. The order matters: you apologise, you name the problem, you make one specific request. Do not stack three requests at once — you will get three answers at speed and be back where you started. Open with Minta maaf. Raise your hand slightly and say Minta maaf.
Your phrasebook marks this as more polite than plain maaf — you are interrupting a class, so use the polite one. Name the problem in one sentence. Say Saya tak faham. Nothing else. This is the single most useful sentence in the room and it is complete on its own. Make one specific request.
Pick exactly one: Boleh ulang? if you missed the content, or Boleh cakap perlahan sikit? if you heard it but could not keep up. Say it once and stop. Ask about the one word you missed. If a single word is the blocker, name it: Apa maksud "tugasan"? The pattern is Apa maksud plus the word.
Tugasan means assignment — your phrasebook lists it alongside kuiz and peperiksaan. Close with Terima kasih. Say Terima kasih when you have your answer. It tells the tutor the problem is solved and the class can move on.
The tutor says, at speed: Tugasan kumpulan perlu dihantar sebelum kelas minggu depan. Student A catches tugasan, kumpulan, kelas, minggu depan — enough to guess there is a group assignment due next week. She nods.
She does not know whether it is before the class or after, does not know the group, and does not know what dihantar means. She finds out on the due date that it had to be submitted online by 5pm on Sunday. Student B raises a hand and says: Minta maaf. Saya tak faham. Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?
The tutor repeats it slower. B still misses dihantar. So: Apa maksud "dihantar"? The tutor says submit and adds, in English, that it goes through the portal. B writes it down. Same class. A leaves with a guess.
B leaves with a deadline, a meaning and a submission method — and the tutor now knows B's name and that B asks.
If I say Saya tak faham in class, the tutor will think I am not trying and mark me down. A tutor cannot teach someone who has silently stopped following, and Saya tak faham is a request, not a confession — the phrasebook puts it in the same list as Boleh ulang? and Boleh cakap perlahan sikit?, all of which are things you say to get help.
The tutor's problem is not that you are lost; it is that they cannot see it. Nodding through a session produces a learner who fails the quiz and never gave the tutor a chance to fix it.

Numbers, money and telling the time.
You are at a mamak table. The waiter says lapan ringgit. You hear lapan and hand over RM 8. He waits. The bill was lapan puluh — eighty. That RM 72 gap is the whole reason this lesson exists. Malay numbers are built from a small set of parts, and the parts are regular.
Learn the ten digits and you can say any price up to 999 without new vocabulary. Three rules generate everything else. Teens add belas. 11 is sebelas (the se- swallows the satu), then 12 dua belas, 13 tiga belas, up to 19 sembilan belas. Tens add puluh. 20 is dua puluh, 30 tiga puluh, 50 lima puluh.
Units come after: 21 is dua puluh satu, 45 is empat puluh lima, 99 is sembilan puluh sembilan. One hundred and one thousand take se-, not satu. 100 is seratus, 1000 is seribu, 1,000,000 is sejuta. But 200 is dua ratus and 2000 is dua ribu. So RM 87 is lapan puluh tujuh ringgit. RM 8 is lapan ringgit.
The difference between them is one word, and it is the word you must not drop. Money: RM is ringgit, and 1 ringgit = 100 sen. RM 4.50 is empat ringgit lima puluh sen. In a shop you will hear kosong for the zero in a phone number or a digit string — 012 reads kosong satu dua. Time is the same arithmetic.
Pukul berapa sekarang? asks the time. Pukul satu is one o'clock, pukul dua setengah is half past two — setengah after the hour means half past, not half to. Days: Isnin, Selasa, Rabu, Khamis, Jumaat, Sabtu, Ahad. Hari ini is today, esok tomorrow, semalam yesterday.
Pagi is morning, tengah hari midday, petang afternoon to dusk, malam night.
The ten digits satu to sepuluh are the only numbers you memorise; everything to 999 is built from them. Teens are formed with belas (tiga belas = 13) and tens with puluh (tiga puluh = 30). Hundreds, thousands and millions take se- for one: seratus, seribu, sejuta — never satu ratus.
Kosong, not sifar, is the zero you say inside a phone number or digit string. 1 ringgit is 100 sen, so RM 4.50 is empat ringgit lima puluh sen. Setengah after the hour means half past: pukul dua setengah is 2:30, not 1:30.
Hari ini, esok and semalam are today, tomorrow and yesterday; pagi, tengah hari, petang and malam split the day.
It is 9 pm at the mamak near Taylor's. You order roti canai and teh tarik. The waiter taps the bill and says a number. You are paying cash and you have a RM 10 note and a RM 100 note in your wallet.
Malay numbers are irregular like English — eleven, twelve and thirteen share nothing, so I just have to memorise each number separately. Malay is regular from 11 upward.
Teens are the digit plus belas (tiga belas = 13), tens are the digit plus puluh (tiga puluh = 30), and only the 'one' forms change, taking se-: sepuluh, sebelas, seratus, seribu, sejuta.
That means once you know satu to sepuluh you can already say 11 to 99 without new vocabulary — the only genuinely irregular-looking items are the se- forms, and there are five of them.

Ordering at the mamak: drinks, food, paying.
You sit down at a mamak. The waiter arrives in about eight seconds and asks "Nak minum apa?" — what do you want to drink. If you say teh, you get hot tea with condensed milk in it. Sweet, milky, and nothing like the plain tea you were picturing. That is the whole problem this lesson solves.
At a mamak the default is sweet and milky, and you have to say extra words to get anything else. Your phrasebook (section 5, "At the mamak") lays out the drink grid. Read it as three switches, not a list of drinks: So teh O kosong is black tea, no milk, no sugar.
Teh tarik is the same milk tea pulled between two cups until it froths — same drink, more air, and it is what the phrasebook's own dialogue has you order. Milo ais is iced Milo, no switches needed. Food works the same way.
Roti canai is flaky flatbread with curry; roti kosong is that bread plain — here kosong means plain, not sugarless, because the word is doing its real job: "nothing added". Roti telur has egg cooked into it. Nasi lemak is coconut rice with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg. Mee goreng mamak is mamak fried noodles.
Kuah campur is mixed curry gravy, and it is how you ask for more than one curry on the plate. Two more words finish the meal. Bungkus means takeaway — tapau means the same thing and comes from Cantonese, so both work. Bang is how you address the waiter; the phrasebook's dialogue ends with "Terima kasih, bang!".
And when you are done: "Bang, kira." That is the bill. Not a question, just the request.
These are the four tea orders you will use most; each can also be made iced with ais. The axis that decides your order is what is in the cup, not what it is called. the learner who has not decided anything yet and wants the safe, sweet, milky cup. sitting down for a proper mamak session rather than a quick drink.
when condensed milk is the thing you cannot face at 8am. studying, or when you have already had three sweet drinks today.
You are at a mamak near campus. Same table, four different days. Day 1. You say "Teh satu." The waiter writes it down. What arrives: hot tea with condensed milk, full sugar. You did not ask for milk. The default put it there. Day 2. You say "Teh O satu." What arrives: hot tea, no milk, sugar still in.
The O removed exactly one thing. Day 3. You say "Teh O kosong satu." What arrives: hot black tea, nothing added. Two switches, two words. Day 4. You say "Teh tarik kurang manis, satu." — the phrasebook's own dialogue line. What arrives: hot pulled milk tea, less sugar than normal.
The milk is still there; kurang manis only touched the sugar. Now the food side, same table: Waiter: Makan? (Anything to eat?) You: Roti canai satu, kuah campur. The satu goes after the dish, the way the phrasebook's dialogue says it. Kuah campur gets you mixed curry rather than one.
If you had said roti kosong you would get the same bread with no egg and no filling — plain. You eat. Then: You: Bang, kira. Waiter: Empat ringgit lima puluh sen. (RM 4.50.) That price is the phrasebook's, from the dialogue in section 5.
You already know empat ringgit lima puluh sen from the numbers and money lesson, so the bill is not a surprise — you can hear it and pay it. If you were taking it home instead of eating there, you would have said bungkus when ordering, or tapau. Same meaning, different word.
You have just sat down at a mamak near Taylor's. It is 9pm, the place is loud, and the waiter is already at your table with his notepad. Order a drink, order food, then ask for the bill.
The word teh just means tea, so if I order teh I get a plain cup of hot tea like at home. At a mamak, teh is the default milk tea: hot tea with condensed milk and sugar already in the cup. Your phrasebook's mamak table gives it as "hot tea with condensed milk (the default)".
To get anything else you add words — teh O removes the milk, kosong removes the sugar, ais makes it cold. The same default logic runs through the food: roti kosong is plain roti, because kosong means "nothing added", not "no sugar".
So the difference it predicts is this: if you order teh expecting plain tea you will be surprised every single time, and if you order teh O kosong expecting plain tea you will get exactly what you wanted.
It is your third day in Malaysia. You are at the mamak two streets from Taylor's with two friends. You have RM 20 in your pocket. You are thirsty, you have not eaten since breakfast, and you have a 2pm class.
